extracted.intended_audience: working men of Paris; general readers interested in political economy
extracted.subtask_description: A nineteenth-century political-economy essay examining whether capital legitimately produces interest and whether that interest may be perpetual; uses examples (sack of corn, house, plane) to illustrate principles of exchange, loan, and value. Written as a didactic argument addressed especially to workers and socialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawfulness of capital producing interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it consistent with the nature of things, and with justice, that capital should produce interest? (author frames this as the primary question and aims to 'prove that it is lawful')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion contrasts economists' assumptions and socialist criticisms (Proudhon, Thoré). Uses examples to show lender performs a service by allowing use of capital and so can demand compensation. Argues denying interest would remove incentive to form capital and harm society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetuity of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it consistent with the nature of things, and with justice, that the interest of capital should be perpetual? (the author treats perpetuity of interest as a separate essential question)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by numerical examples (e.g., 20,000 francs at 5% producing repeated income across centuries) and by argument that lending (even of consumables) can yield perpetual returns because repayment enables re-lending; examines social consequences of denying perpetual interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital is composed of three things: (1) materials upon which men operate that already have value (wool, flax, leather, silk, wood, &c.); (2) instruments used for working--tools, machines, ships, carriages, &c.; (3) provisions consumed during labour--victuals, stuffs, houses, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because capital consists of materials, instruments, and provisions (not merely money), it can legitimately be exchanged, sold, lent, and produce remuneration when used; this definition underpins later arguments about lending and interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of value: reciprocity of services
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of value is in the services rendered and received on account of the productions exchanged, rather than in the productions themselves ('exchange is the reciprocity of services').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained via examples (Paul's coat sold for money then used to buy goods; J. B. Say quote). Implies that fairness of exchange should be judged by whether services are reciprocated, not by intrinsic properties of goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable exchange results from liberty (free voluntary agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: To render the exchange 'equitable' the best means was to allow it to be free; 'equal value results from liberty.' State intervention on one side or the other is oppressive and distorts appreciation of value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The State's proper role is to prevent artifice and fraud and secure liberty, not to fix or interfere with voluntary bargains. This is the evaluative standard for whether exchanges are just.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair loan terms: restoration of same quality and compensation for use
rubrics_metrics.description: When a consumable is lent, the lender may legitimately require (a) that it be returned in the same quality/weight (so the lender does not 'give'), and (b) compensation corresponding to the borrower's gains from using it (e.g., 'He engaged to deliver five litres on every hectolitre').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fair loan thus contains at least two clauses: repayment (preserve equality of the principal) and a compensation clause for the use/delay. The sack-of-corn anecdote illustrates that charging a share of produced surplus is just because the lender enabled the borrower's profitable enterprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest/credit as two services (exchange + compensation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A loan can be analysed as two exchanges: (1) the initial exchange (principal), and (2) the delay/grant of use by one party with a corresponding compensatory service by the other; these two services are called 'credit' and 'interest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming does not change nature: both are services requiring reciprocity. This analysis justifies interest as the compensatory service equivalent to the lender's granting of delayed possession or use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lender's right to compensation for deprivation of use (examples: house, plane)
rubrics_metrics.description: When one party uses another's capital (house, tool), it is just that the user bear the consequences of wear/repairs and render an equivalent service or compensation to the owner; the owner may demand replacement, repair-costs, or further compensation beyond mere return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: House example: occupant must quit at year's end, restore house save ordinary decay, reimburse architect's annual repairs, and render an equivalent service agreed by free negotiation. Plane example: maker who created a tool to improve his work can justly demand compensation if another uses it for the period when the maker would otherwise have benefited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital is distinct from money
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital is not money; although some imagine capital is money and thus deny its productiveness, in fact capital pre-dates precious metals and includes materials, tools and provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction undermines arguments that 'crowns cannot reproduce themselves'—productiveness of capital rests on its use in production, not on coins in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the State: secure liberty and repress fraud, not set exchange terms
rubrics_metrics.description: It ought to be the part of the State to prevent, and, above all, to repress artifice and fraud; that is, to secure liberty, and not to violate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State interference to fix prices or force gratuitous loans is condemned as oppressive and likely to harm one contracting party; protecting free bargaining is the standard for just economic arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of inheritance as legitimate form of property transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of inheritance is one of the forms of gift and 'the most natural of all'; what a man has produced he may consume, exchange, or give, including to his children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inheritance incentivizes labour and saving; objections that inheritance plunders the masses are rejected by political economy's claim that value produced harms no one and may be transmitted without injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: When delivery is delayed in an otherwise equal exchange, compensation is just
rubrics_metrics.description: If an originally equal exchange is modified by delaying the other party's delivery (e.g., exchange of house for ship but possession of the ship delayed a year), the delayed possession constitutes a new service that justly requires equivalent compensation to restore fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the modified transaction as two transactions: the original exchange plus the compensation for the delay (credit/interest). This is the standard to judge whether added clauses are injurious or equitable.
